entry: Chinese-American theoretical physicist. With Tsung-Dao Lee he proposed that parity is not conserved in the [[Weak interaction|weak interaction]], for which the two shared the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1954 he and Robert Mills developed non-Abelian gauge theory, known as [[Yang–Mills theory]], which underlies the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics. Yang also worked on [[Statistical mechanics|statistical mechanics]], integrable systems and condensed matter physics. He studied under Edward Teller and worked as an assistant to Enrico Fermi at the [[University of Chicago]]. After first visiting mainland China in 1971, he helped rebuild its physics research community, and he later served as an honorary director of [[Tsinghua University]].

sort_key: yang mills existence and mass gap
entry: Unsolved problem in mathematical physics, one of the seven [[Millennium Prize Problems]]. It asks for a proof that, for any compact simple gauge group, a non-trivial quantum [[Yang–Mills theory]] exists on four-dimensional Euclidean space and that the mass of every predicted particle is strictly positive (a mass gap). The Clay Mathematics Institute offers US$1,000,000 for a solution. On October 26, 2026, OpenAI announced an AI-generated proof of the existence part, which an independent team led by David Gross verified. The mass gap remains unproven.

Quantum field theory based on non-Abelian gauge groups. Devised by Chen Ning Yang and Robert Mills as a theory of nuclear binding, the term now covers a class of similar theories. It is a [[Gauge theory|gauge theory]] based on the special unitary group SU(n) or any compact Lie group. These theories unify the electromagnetic and weak forces (U(1) × SU(2)) and form the basis of [[Quantum chromodynamics]], the theory of the strong force (based on SU(3)), so they underpin the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics.

Largest city and principal commercial center of [[Myanmar]]. Founded as Dagon by the Mon people in the early 11th century, it was renamed Yangon in 1755 by [[Alaungpaya]], founder of the [[Konbaung dynasty]]. The British captured it in 1852 and built a grid-plan city that became the hub of British Burma. Yangon has the largest number of colonial-era buildings in Southeast Asia, and the gilded Shwedagon Pagoda is Myanmar's most sacred Buddhist pagoda. It was the capital until 2006, when the military government moved administrative functions to Naypyidaw. With over five million people, the city suffers from inadequate infrastructure compared with [[Jakarta]], [[Bangkok]] and [[Hanoi]].

Chinese basketball executive and former player. Born in [[Shanghai]], he played for the Shanghai Sharks before the Houston Rockets made him the first overall pick in the 2002 NBA draft. Over nine seasons in the [[National Basketball Association]] he was an eight-time All-Star and was named to the All-NBA Team five times. In 2016 he became the first Chinese national inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame, alongside [[Shaquille O'Neal]] and [[Allen Iverson]]. He was elected chairman of the Chinese Basketball Association in 2017.

Capital of [[Cameroon]] and its second-largest city after the port of [[Douala]]. It lies in the Centre Region at about 750 meters (2,500 ft) above sea level and has more than 2.8 million people. German explorers established a trading post there in 1887 for rubber and ivory, and a military garrison built in 1895 enabled further colonization. After World War I, France administered eastern Cameroon as a [[League of Nations]] mandate and made Yaoundé the colonial capital in 1922. It remained the seat of government after independence in 1960. The economy centers on the civil service, and industries include [[Tobacco|tobacco]], [[Dairy|dairy]] products, beer, [[Clay|clay]], glass goods and timber.

Long continuous length of interlocked fibers used in sewing, [[Knitting|knitting]], [[Weaving|weaving]], embroidery and rope-making. Yarn can be spun from natural fibers such as [[Cotton]], [[Silk]], linen and [[Wool]], or from synthetics such as [[Nylon]] and [[Polyester]]. Cotton is the most common plant fiber, and wool the most common spun animal fiber. Yarn production dates to the Stone Age, and silk thread was well established in China by the [[Shang dynasty]]. Thread is a yarn intended for sewing by hand or machine, and modern sewing thread is often finished with wax to withstand the stresses of sewing. Yarn comes in many colors and thicknesses, called weights, and most yarns are solid colored.

Grand Prince of [[Kyiv|Kiev]] (r. 1019–1054). Son of [[Vladimir the Great]] and Rogneda of Polotsk, he ruled Rostov and then Novgorod before winning the Kievan throne in 1019 after a war against his half-brother Sviatopolk. As grand prince he forged alliances with Scandinavian countries, weakened Byzantine influence in Kiev, and captured the area around present-day Tartu, [[Estonia]]. He defended his state against the Pechenegs with a line of forts. He was a patron of literature, sponsoring the construction of Saint Sophia Cathedral in 1037 and promoting the first work of Old East Slavic literature. Several of his daughters married into foreign royal families. After his death his body was placed in a sarcophagus in Saint Sophia's Cathedral.

Indian actor and film producer in [[Kannada]] cinema, known in the media as the "Rocking Star". He made his film debut in 2007, and his performance in the 2008 romantic drama *Moggina Manasu* won the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor. Leading roles in *Googly* and *Raja Huli* (both 2013) made him a commercial star. The *KGF* films, *KGF: Chapter 1* (2018) and *KGF: Chapter 2* (2022), brought him nationwide recognition, and the second is the highest-grossing Kannada film. He is married to actress [[Radhika Pandit]], with whom he has two children, and he runs the Yasho Marga Foundation.

Palestinian political leader and chairman of the [[Palestine Liberation Organization]] (PLO) from 1969. Born in Cairo to Palestinian parents, he fought alongside the [[Muslim Brotherhood]] in the [[1948 Arab–Israeli War]] and co-founded Fatah in the late 1950s, a group that sought Israel's replacement with a Palestinian state. Based in [[Tunisia]] from 1983 to 1993, he began to pursue negotiation, and in 1988 he acknowledged Israel's right to exist. The [[Oslo Accords]] of 1993 earned him, with [[Yitzhak Rabin]] and [[Shimon Peres]], the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize. He was president of the Palestinian Authority from 1994 and president of Palestine from 1989 until 2004. Palestinians generally viewed him as a national symbol, while many Israelis regarded him as a terrorist.

Japanese film director whose quiet dramas of family life are among the most admired in world cinema. He began in the silent era with short comedies and turned to more serious themes in the 1930s. His films focus on family and marriage, and especially on relationships between generations, notably *Late Spring* (1949), [[Tokyo Story]] (1953) and *An Autumn Afternoon* (1962). In the 2012 *Sight & Sound* poll, 358 directors named *Tokyo Story* the greatest film of all time. His static, low-angled camera and avoidance of conventional transitions gave his work a distinctive style. Wim Wenders's documentary *Tokyo-Ga* (1985) is among several films about him.

Japanese novelist and short-story writer whose spare, lyrical prose won the 1968 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first awarded to a Japanese author. Orphaned young, he studied at the [[University of Tokyo]], where he published his first short story in 1921. In 1924 he helped found the literary journal *Bungei Jidai* as a reaction against the entrenched old schools. As a student he was drawn to the work of [[Rabindranath Tagore]]. His major works include *Snow Country* (1935–1937), about a geisha's futile romance in a remote hot-spring town, and *Thousand Cranes* (1949–1951), on inheritance and desire in the tea ceremony. His works have broad international appeal and remain widely read.

Japanese artist known for sculpture, installation and obsessively repeated motifs such as polka dots, nets and [[Pumpkin|pumpkins]]. Rooted in conceptual art, her work also includes painting, performance and fashion. After moving to [[New York City]] in 1958 she joined the avant-garde scene of the 1960s and was associated with [[Pop art]]; her work influenced contemporaries including [[Andy Warhol]]. Happenings she organized, in which nude participants were painted with polka dots, brought her public attention. She voluntarily lived in a [[Tokyo]] psychiatric hospital from 1977, crediting art with helping her cope with mental illness. Renewed interest from the late 1980s led to major retrospectives worldwide.

Software flaw, known as Y2K, arising from storing calendar years as two digits, which risked reading the year 2000 as 1900. Individual companies predicted that repairs would cost between $400 billion and $600 billion worldwide, and fears of a computer-induced [[Apocalypse|apocalypse]] led some people to stockpile food and cash. Few major errors occurred. Supporters credited the preemptive work of programmers, and U.S. President [[Bill Clinton]] called Y2K "the first challenge of the 21st century successfully met". Critics argued that problems were minimal even in countries that had done little to prepare.

Informal group of single-celled [[Fungus|fungi]] that reproduce mainly by budding or fission. Yeasts are eukaryotic microorganisms, with at least 1,500 recognized species, and form about 1% of described fungal species. Yeast microbes are probably among the earliest domesticated organisms. The species *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* converts sugars to carbon dioxide and ethanol through [[Fermentation|fermentation]], a process used in baking and brewing for thousands of years. It is also a [[Model organism|model organism]] in cell biology research. Other species, such as *Candida albicans*, are opportunistic [[Pathogen|pathogens]], and yeasts are used to produce ethanol for the [[Biofuel|biofuel]] industry. Yeasts are placed in two separate phyla, the [[Ascomycota]] and the [[Basidiomycota]].

Administrative center and largest city of Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russia. Located on the Iset River between the Volga-Ural region and [[Siberia]], it has roughly 1.5 million residents and is the fourth most populous city in Russia. Founded in 1723 and named after Catherine, wife of [[Peter the Great]], it became the mining capital of the Russian Empire. It was the site of the murder of the Romanov family, including Tsar [[Nicholas II]], during the [[Russian Civil War]]. Renamed Sverdlovsk in 1924, it regained its historical name in 1991. Yekaterinburg is known for its constructivist architecture and was one of the host cities of the 2018 FIFA World Cup.

Color between [[Green|green]] and [[Orange (colour)|orange]] on the visible spectrum of light, evoked by a dominant wavelength of roughly 575–585 nm. It is a primary color in subtractive systems such as [[CMYK color model|CMYK]] printing, while in the [[RGB color model|RGB]] model used for screens it is made by combining red and green light. Carotenoid pigments give yellow to autumn leaves, corn, daffodils and bananas. Yellow ochre was one of the first colors used in art, and a painting of a yellow horse in France's Lascaux cave is about 17,000 years old. In the early Christian church yellow was associated with [[Judas Iscariot]] and used to mark heretics. Surveys in Europe, Canada and the United States associate yellow with amusement, gentleness and happiness, but also with jealousy and cowardice.

Legendary Chinese sovereign and culture hero, one of the [[Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors]]. He is traditionally regarded as the initiator of Chinese culture and credited with the traditional calendar, [[Taoism]], wooden houses, boats, carts, the compass needle and the earliest forms of writing. Texts such as the *Huangdi Neijing*, a medical classic, were attributed to him, and he is associated with [[Traditional Chinese medicine]]. His cult is first attested in the [[Warring States period]]. In the early twentieth century he became a rallying figure for Han Chinese attempts to overthrow the [[Qing dynasty]], and he remains a symbol of Chinese nationalism. Most historians treat him as a legendary rather than a historical ruler.

Second-longest river in [[China]] and the sixth-longest in the world, flowing about 5,464 km to the Bohai Sea. It is named for the yellow color of its water, which comes from the sediment it picks up on the Loess Plateau. Rising in the Bayan Har Mountains, it loops around the Ordos Plateau and crosses the [[North China Plain]]. The basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese civilization, and the [[Xia dynasty]] is traditionally said to have originated on its banks. Its frequent floods have earned it the nicknames "China's Pride" and "China's Sorrow"; one estimate counts 1,593 floods between 595 BC and 1946. The basin supports about 120 million people, and since 2003 China has built the South–North Water Transfer Project to ease strain on its water supply.

Marginal sea of the western [[Pacific Ocean]] between mainland [[China]] and the Korean Peninsula. It is one of four seas named after color terms, with the [[Black Sea]], [[Red Sea]] and [[White Sea]], and its name describes the golden-yellow silt discharged by rivers such as the [[Yellow River]]. The sea is shallow, with an area of about 380,000 sq km and an average depth of only 44 m. It is a flooded section of continental shelf that formed as sea levels rose after the last glacial period. Winters are cold and dry under northerly monsoon winds, and fog is frequent along the coasts. The sea forms the northwestern part of the [[East China Sea]].

Viral disease of typically short duration, spread by the bite of an infected [[Mosquito|mosquito]]. Most cases cause fever, chills, headache, back pain and nausea, and symptoms typically improve within five days. In about 15% of cases a toxic phase follows, with recurring fever, [[Jaundice]] from liver damage, abdominal pain and bleeding. Among those who develop jaundice the fatality rate is 20%–50%. There is no specific treatment, but a safe and effective [[Vaccine|vaccine]] exists, and reducing mosquito populations helps prevention. The disease originated in Africa and is common in tropical parts of Africa and South America. The yellow fever virus became the first human virus to be isolated, in 1927.

Populist grassroots movement of weekly protests in [[France]] from 2018 to 2020. It began in November 2018 over rising fuel prices. Protesters demanded lower fuel taxes, a return of the solidarity tax on wealth and a minimum wage increase, and some sought the resignation of President [[Emmanuel Macron]]. The yellow high-visibility vests that French law requires motorists to carry became a worldwide protest symbol. Blockades and riots, some the most violent since [[May 68]], damaged landmarks such as the [[Arc de Triomphe]], and police tactics were criticized. About 3 million people took part before the protests ended during the COVID-19 pandemic.

North American name for social [[Wasp|wasps]] of the genera *Vespula* and *Dolichovespula*. Most are black and yellow, and all females can sting. Yellowjackets are predators that help control pest insects. They live in annual colonies, with fertilized queens overwintering alone to start new colonies in spring, and they build papery nests from chewed wood fiber. Often mistaken for [[Honey bee|honey bees]], they lack the dense hair and pollen-carrying legs of bees, and they can sting repeatedly.

[[National park]] in the western United States, located mainly in northwest [[Wyoming]] with parts in Montana and Idaho. Established in 1872 by an act signed by President [[Ulysses S. Grant]], it was the first national park in the world. Well over half of the world's [[Geyser|geysers]] and hydrothermal features are here, fueled by the [[Caldera|Yellowstone Caldera]], a dormant volcano. The park is home to [[Grizzly bear|grizzly bears]], cougars, wolves and herds of [[Bison]] and elk. Forest fires burned over one-third of the park in 1988. Yellowstone was named a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1978 and is the centerpiece of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem.

Cossack ataman who led Pugachev's Rebellion, a major uprising against [[Catherine the Great]]. Son of a Don Cossack landowner, he served in the Russian army in the [[Seven Years' War]], deserted in 1770 and lived for years as a fugitive. In 1773 he proclaimed himself Tsar Peter III, Catherine's late husband, and promised an end to [[Serfdom|serfdom]]. His forces overran much of the region between the [[Volga]] and the Urals and in 1774 captured and burned [[Kazan]]. After a crushing defeat, he was captured by his own Cossacks and turned over to the authorities. He was executed in [[Moscow]]. [[Alexander Pushkin]] wrote a history of the rebellion and recounted it in his novel *The Captain's Daughter* (1836).
